title: 007 — .NET 11 Release Candidate 2: the last stop before GA
html:
007 — .NET 11 Release Candidate 2: the last stop before GA

The one idea: .NET 11 RC2 is the final release candidate and carries a go-live licence, so you can run it in production with Microsoft support. It is the right moment to build your apps on .NET 11 and find breaking changes before GA. The new pieces are small but useful: incremental CBOR reading, post-quantum and HPKE crypto previews, cleaner validation messages, HTTP/2 tuning, and better dotnet run for file-based apps.

Added 2026-10-14 · Released 2026-10-13 by Microsoft

1. What it is

RC2 is the second and final release candidate of .NET 11. The feature set is locked. What's left before GA is mostly fixes. The highlights by area:

Area Change
Libraries CborReader can read a payload that arrives in chunks
Libraries Experimental CompositeMLKem (post-quantum plus classical key exchange) and Hpke (Hybrid Public Key Encryption)
Libraries ValidationAttribute.FormatMessage for localized DataAnnotations messages
Libraries SocketsHttpHandler.InitialHttp2MaxConcurrentStreams
ASP.NET Core QuickGrid virtualization APIs are no longer experimental
SDK Quoted values and item metadata in file-level #: directives
SDK MSBuild properties such as $(AssemblyName) expand in launch-profile arguments
Runtime File locking disabled by default on iOS and tvOS
.NET MAUI C# UI app template, Apple Icon Composer assets, XAML authoring and Hot Reload work

2. Why it matters

  • Go-live means production is allowed. Teams that want to ship on .NET 11 from day one can start now, not after GA.
  • Last chance to report breaking changes. If something breaks on RC2, it is much easier to get it fixed before GA than after.
  • Streaming data without big buffers. Incremental CBOR reading lets an API or IoT gateway parse a large payload chunk by chunk, so it never has to copy the whole document into one array.
  • Getting ready for post-quantum crypto. Composite ML-KEM pairs a post-quantum algorithm with a classical one, so the secret stays safe even if one of them is broken. It's experimental, but you can start designing for it.
  • Cleaner validation in multi-language apps. A host can supply a translated message template, and the attribute fills in its own values.

3. How it works

---
title: Incremental CBOR reading
---
sequenceDiagram
    participant N as Network stream
    participant R as CborReader (Lax, isFinalBlock false)
    participant A as App code
    N->>R: chunk 1
    A->>R: ReadStartArray, ReadInt32
    R-->>A: NeedsMoreData
    N->>R: SlideData(chunk 2, isFinalBlock true)
    A->>R: ReadInt32, ReadEndArray

The reader keeps its place between chunks. When it runs out of bytes, PeekState() returns CborReaderState.NeedsMoreData. You hand it the next chunk with SlideData, and it carries on.

4. How to use it

Install the .NET 11 RC2 SDK. Then set <TargetFramework>net11.0</TargetFramework> on a branch and run your tests.

Incremental CBOR (from the release notes):

var reader = new CborReader(chunk1,
    new CborReaderOptions { ConformanceMode = CborConformanceMode.Lax }, isFinalBlock: false);
reader.ReadStartArray();
int first = reader.ReadInt32();
if (reader.PeekState() == CborReaderState.NeedsMoreData)
    reader.SlideData(chunk2, isFinalBlock: true);
int second = reader.ReadInt32();
reader.ReadEndArray();

Validation messages:

var range = new RangeAttribute(1, 10);
string message = range.FormatMessage("{0} must be between {1} and {2}", "Value");
// Value must be between 1 and 10

HTTP/2 burst control. Set SocketsHttpHandler.InitialHttp2MaxConcurrentStreams (default 100, minimum 1). This caps the streams a new connection opens before the server's SETTINGS frame arrives. Once the frame arrives, the server's own limit applies.

File-based apps. Directives now accept quoted values and metadata:

#:property Company="Platform Team"
#:package System.CommandLine@2.0.1 Aliases=CommandLine

Launch profiles. commandLineArgs such as --name $(AssemblyName) are now expanded when you run dotnet run --launch-profile <name>.

In practice, an upgrade checklist:

  1. Read "Breaking changes in .NET 11" on Microsoft Learn before you change the target framework.
  2. Build with warnings as errors and fix any new analyzer warnings.
  3. Run the integration tests and a load test. Compare memory and latency with the current version.
  4. Check that your hosting platform (Azure App Service, Functions, container base images) offers .NET 11 before you plan the production date.

5. Trade-offs and limits

  • The crypto APIs are experimental. Using them means opting in to diagnostic IDs SYSLIB5006 (Composite ML-KEM) and SYSLIB5009 (HPKE). The APIs may still change. RC2's HPKE supports only the classical DHKEM suites. The ML-KEM suites aren't there yet.
  • Incremental CBOR needs Lax mode. Strict conformance modes reject non-final blocks.
  • Go-live isn't GA. You get support, but expect at least one more round of fixes. Pin the SDK version with global.json so builds stay repeatable.
  • Adopt now or wait? Upgrade a branch now and run CI on it. Move production at GA, unless you need a .NET 11 feature sooner and can keep up with patches.

6. Where it fits

  • .NET deep dive: runtime and framework basics behind each release.
  • C# performance: how to measure before and after an upgrade.
  • Encryption in practice: where key encapsulation and hybrid encryption fit.
  • Networking fundamentals: HTTP/2 streams and flow control.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. What does a go-live licence allow, and how is it different from GA?
  2. Why does incremental CBOR reading need CborConformanceMode.Lax?
  3. Why combine a post-quantum KEM with a classical one, not replace one with the other?
  4. When would you lower InitialHttp2MaxConcurrentStreams below 100?
  5. What would you check before moving an Azure-hosted API to .NET 11?
